"In one's cups" means to be drunk — that is, to have consumed enough alcohol that it has visibly affected a person's behavior, speech, or judgment.

When someone is in their cups, they are intoxicated. They might be talking too loudly, saying things they normally wouldn't, stumbling, or acting in a way that is clearly influenced by alcohol.

"Don't argue with him tonight — he's in his cups."
(= He is drunk, so arguing with him is pointless.)

The key word here is "cups." In older times, a "cup" wasn't just any cup — it specifically referred to a cup filled with an alcoholic drink, usually wine or ale. Drinking from such a cup meant consuming alcohol.

So if a person was in their cups, it painted a picture of someone who had been drinking cup after cup after cup of alcohol — so much so that the alcohol now had them "in its grip," so to speak.

Think of it this way:

  • One cup → fine.
  • Two cups → still okay.
  • Many cups → now you are in your cups.

The phrase captures the idea that the person has been consumed by their drinking, rather than the other way around.

This is an ancient expression. One of its earliest recorded uses appears in 1 Esdras, a text from the Biblical Apocrypha (written roughly in the 3rd–2nd century BCE), where it says that men in their cups forget their love for friends and brothers and even draw out swords — meaning alcohol makes people forget themselves entirely.

The idiom has been in continuous use in English literature since at least the 16th century, appearing in the works of writers across many generations. It is one of those rare phrases that has survived for over two thousand years.
The Tone of This Idiom — This Is Important

One crucial thing to understand is that "in one's cups" is not a harsh or aggressive phrase. It carries a tone that is:

  • Old-fashioned and literary — it sounds refined and almost gentle.
  • Slightly humorous or wry — it treats drunkenness with a kind of knowing, soft amusement rather than harsh judgment.
  • Tactful — it is often used when a speaker wants to point out someone's drunkenness without being rude or blunt about it.

Compare the following ways of saying the same thing:

ExpressionTone
"He's drunk."Plain and direct
"He's wasted / hammered / smashed."Casual, slang, slightly harsh
"He's in his cups."Old-fashioned, literary, gently humorous

Choosing "in his cups" instead of "he's drunk" immediately gives the sentence a more elegant, almost forgiving flavor. It softens the observation.
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

The idiom always appears with a possessive pronoun that refers to the person who is drunk:

  • in his cups (he is drunk)
  • in her cups (she is drunk)
  • in their cups (they are drunk)
  • in my cups (I am drunk)
  • in one's cups (the general/neutral form)

You would never say "in the cups" or "in cups" — the possessive is non-negotiable.

It is used after a verb like "be" (is, was, were, are):

✅ "She was in her cups by midnight."
✅ "He tends to make promises when he's in his cups."
✅ "They were clearly in their cups at the party."
❌ "He in-his-cups arrived." ← This doesn't work grammatically.

This is a nuance worth noting. The idiom doesn't describe:

  • Barely tipsy — that would be too mild.
  • Completely passed out unconscious — that would typically be described differently.

It describes that middle zone of noticeable drunkenness — where the person is awake and functioning, but their behavior, speech, and judgment are clearly affected by alcohol. They might be overly emotional, too talkative, making poor decisions, or saying things they'll regret the next morning.

Here are examples that show the idiom being used naturally:

  1. "Pay no attention to what he said about you — he was in his cups and talking nonsense."

(= He was drunk and not speaking sense.)

  1. "She only ever sings at parties when she's in her cups."

(= Alcohol loosens her up enough to sing.)

  1. "The old general, in his cups, would tell long stories about the war."

(= When drunk, the old general would ramble about the war.)

  1. "I regret sending that message. I was in my cups and not thinking clearly."

(= I was drunk when I sent it.)

  1. "He made a grand speech in his cups, promising everyone the world."

(= While drunk, he made exaggerated promises.)
When Would You Actually Use This Phrase?

In modern spoken language, people rarely say "in one's cups" in casual everyday conversation — they'd more likely say "drunk," "tipsy," or use slang. However, you will encounter this idiom frequently in:

  • Literature — especially older novels, plays, and poetry.
  • Formal or elevated writing — where the writer wants a sophisticated, old-world feel.
  • Humorous writing — where the dated sound of the phrase adds a wry, comedic touch.
  • Journalism and essays — when a writer wants to describe drunkenness with some elegance.

So even if you don't use it in everyday speech yourself, you need to recognize it when you read it, especially in classic literature.

In short: if you read that someone was "in their cups," picture them sitting at a table, having had far too many drinks, their cheeks flushed, their words a little too free — drunk enough that they're not quite themselves anymore. That is exactly what this elegant old idiom means.
